title: Goecha La trek: route, permits, costs and kit
meta_description: Plan the Goecha La trek from Yuksom: day-by-day route, altitudes, best months, park and foreign trekker permits, agency costs, acclimatisation and kit.
summary: The Goecha La trek starts and ends at Yuksom, covers about 90 km in 8–9 walking days and climbs to Viewpoint 1 at about 4,600 m, facing Kangchenjunga. You must go with a registered agency and licensed guide. Group treks cost ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative 2026. The best months are April–May and October–November.

sections.heading: The route in brief
paras: The trek follows the Rathong Chu valley north from Yuksom (1,780 m) into Khangchendzonga National Park. It climbs through oak, magnolia and rhododendron forest to Sachen and Tshoka, then above the tree line to the yak pastures of Dzongri at about 4,020 m. From there it drops into the Prek Chu valley at Kokchurang, follows the river up to Thansing and Lamuney, passes Samiti Lake at about 4,200 m and ends below the south-east face of Kangchenjunga.

The pass itself, Goecha La, is at 4,940 m by Wikipedia's figure. Most groups now finish at Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, and return the same way. The full round trip is about 90 km on foot. Our Dzongri and Goecha La place page covers the camps and views in more detail; this guide is about planning.
The park is large: about 1,784 km², set up in 1977 and listed by UNESCO in 2016 as India's first 'mixed' World Heritage Site, for both its nature and its cultural meaning.

sections.heading: Day-by-day outline
paras: Most agencies run the trek over 10–11 days door to door from Siliguri, with 8–9 days on foot. The outline below is typical; some groups shorten it by walking straight from Yuksom to Tshoka on day 2, which we do not recommend for first-timers because it gains about 1,200 m in a day. Distances are approximate.

sections.heading: Best months and weather
paras: There are two seasons. Spring, from April to mid-May, brings rhododendrons in flower between Tshoka and Dzongri and milder nights, but cloud often builds by late morning and views are best at dawn. Autumn, from late September to November, is the clearest time of year; October mornings at Dzongri can be spotless, though nights can drop to around -5 °C to -10 °C higher up.

From December to February heavy snow above Dzongri closes the route in practice. Agencies do not run it from June to August, when the monsoon brings leeches, landslides and almost no views. Late May and September are possible but are a gamble on weather.

sections.heading: Permits and the rules on the trail
paras: This is not a trek you can walk alone. The rules as we understand them are below; they are revised often, so check current status before you travel.

The Viewpoint 1 question needs a clear answer before you pay. In recent seasons most groups have turned back at Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, and the walk on towards Viewpoint 2 and the pass has been restricted by the forest department. Ask your agency in writing where your group will be allowed to go this season, and do not book with anyone who promises the pass without explaining the current rule.
list: Trek with a registered agency and a licensed local guide; solo trekking is not permitted.
Khangchendzonga National Park entry and camping fees are paid at the forest checkpost in Yuksom; amounts change, and your agency usually handles them.
Indian nationals carry an original photo ID and copies; no other permit is needed for West Sikkim.
Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, free and valid 30 days, from e-FRRO online or at Melli or Rangpo checkposts.
Foreign nationals also need a trek permit for the park, arranged only through a registered agency and normally for groups of two or more.
Huts at Sachen, Tshoka, Dzongri, Thansing and Lamuney are basic and shared; most agencies also use tents.

sections.heading: What it costs
paras: Group departures with a registered agency cost about ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative 2026, from Yuksom. That usually covers food, tents or huts, guide, cook, porters or pack animals and park permits. A private trek for two costs ₹35,000 or more per person. A packaged trip from Siliguri with transfers and Yuksom hotel nights runs about ₹22,000–26,000 per person on a budget, ₹30,000–36,000 in comfort, and ₹55,000–70,000 for a private trek, indicative 2026.

To save money, travel to Yuksom by shared jeep: Siliguri to Gyalshing costs ₹400–550 a seat, then Gyalshing to Yuksom ₹120–180, indicative 2026. Rent sleeping bags, down jackets and poles in Yuksom rather than buying. Check whether your fare includes carrying your rucksack; if not, agree the extra charge before you start. Tip the guide, cook and porters at the end; ask your agency what is usual.

Arrive in Yuksom a day early if you can. It gives you a night at 1,780 m before the climb, time to meet your guide and check the gear, and a buffer if the road from Siliguri is slow. Budget rooms such as Hotel Yangrigang on the main road suit trekkers, and village homestays cost about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a day with meals, indicative 2026. Keep one night spare at the end too, in case a landslide closes the road out.

sections.heading: Altitude sickness and acclimatisation
paras: The big risk on Goecha La is altitude, not the walking. You sleep above 4,000 m on several nights, and acute mountain sickness can hit fit young people as easily as anyone. Early signs are headache, nausea, poor sleep, loss of appetite and unusual tiredness. Tell your guide at once; it is not a weakness.

Our rules are simple. Keep the rest day at Dzongri. Walk slowly enough to talk. Drink 3–4 litres of water a day. Do not go higher with symptoms, and go down if they get worse. Confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest are emergencies; descend immediately. Talk to your doctor before the trip about acetazolamide and any heart, lung or blood-pressure condition. Start walking or running 4–6 weeks beforehand; you should manage 5 km in about 35 minutes.

sections.heading: Kit list and leaving no trace
paras: Pack light; a porter or pack animal carries the main load and you carry a day pack of about 6–8 kg. These are the items we would never leave behind.
list: Ankle-high trekking shoes with good grip, worn in before the trip.
Three warm layers plus a down jacket; thermal tops and bottoms for nights.
Waterproof jacket and trousers, and a poncho or rucksack cover.
Woollen cap, sun cap, gloves (inner and waterproof outer), 3–4 pairs of woollen socks.
UV sunglasses, sunscreen SPF 50, lip balm and a headlamp with spare batteries.
Two 1-litre bottles, a small personal first-aid kit and your own medicines.
A trash bag: carry out every wrapper, battery and tissue; Sikkim's forests are not a dustbin.
Use toilet tents or dig catholes well away from streams; never wash with soap in a stream or at Samiti Lake.

sections.heading: The mountain and its story
paras: For the Lepcha, the oldest people of Sikkim, Kangchenjunga is Kongchen Kongchlo. In Lepcha tradition the first Lepcha man and woman were made from the snows of its summit. For Sikkim as a whole it is a guardian deity, honoured each year at Pang Lhabsol.

That respect shaped climbing history. On 25 May 1955 the Britons Joe Brown and George Band made the first ascent from the Nepal side, but stopped a few feet short of the true summit. They were keeping a promise made to Sikkim's ruler, Chogyal Tashi Namgyal, that the top would stay untrodden. Norman Hardie and Tony Streather reached the same point the next day. The Indian side is closed to climbing expeditions, which is why you can look at the face from Goecha La but not climb it. Treat the lakes and chortens along the trail the same way: walk around them clockwise and keep them clean.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Moderate to difficult. You walk 5–7 hours on most days for 8–9 days and sleep above 4,000 m on several nights. The summit day to Viewpoint 1 takes 10–12 hours. The trail is not technical, but altitude makes it hard. Fit first-timers who train for 4–6 weeks and keep the Dzongri rest day usually manage well.

faqs.q: Can I do the Goecha La trek without a guide
faqs.a: No. The trek runs through Khangchendzonga National Park, and the rules require you to go with a registered agency and a licensed local guide. Park entry and camping fees are paid at the Yuksom forest checkpost. Foreign nationals also need a trek permit arranged by a registered agency. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are trekkers allowed to go to Goecha La pass
faqs.a: In recent seasons most groups have turned back at Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, and access beyond it towards Viewpoint 2 and the pass at 4,940 m has been restricted by the forest department. Rules change from season to season. Ask your agency in writing what is allowed this year and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does the Goecha La trek cost
faqs.a: Group departures with a registered agency cost about ₹14,000–25,000 per person from Yuksom, indicative 2026, covering food, camps, guide, cook, porters or pack animals and permits. Private treks start around ₹35,000 per person. Add travel to Yuksom: about ₹520–730 by shared jeep from Siliguri via Gyalshing, or ₹5,500–7,500 to Pelling by reserved car.

faqs.q: What is the best month for the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: October and early November give the clearest views of Kangchenjunga and the most stable weather, with cold nights. April and early May bring rhododendrons in bloom and milder temperatures, but more afternoon cloud. The route is closed by snow in practice from December to February, and agencies do not run it from June to August.

faqs.q: Do foreigners need a special permit for Goecha La
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which is free and valid for 30 days, from e-FRRO or at Melli or Rangpo checkposts. On top of that they need a trek permit for Khangchendzonga National Park, arranged through a registered agency and normally for groups of two or more. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Goecha La
faqs.a: Plan 10–11 days from Siliguri or NJP and back: one day's drive each way to Yuksom and 8–9 days on foot, including a rest day at Dzongri. Add a spare day for weather or road delays. Shorter itineraries cut out the rest day and raise the risk of altitude sickness.

Goecha La pass is at 4,940 m by Wikipedia's figure. Viewpoint 1, where most groups now end the trek, is at about 4,600 m. The highest night is usually at Lamuney, about 4,150 m, or at Dzongri, about 4,020 m. Yuksom, the start, is at 1,780 m, so you gain over 2,800 m.

faqs.q: Where can I rent trekking gear for Goecha La
faqs.a: Yuksom has several shops and agencies that rent sleeping bags, down jackets, trekking poles, and gaiters for a modest daily fee. Many agencies include a sleeping bag in the fare. Bring your own worn-in shoes, socks and base layers, and inspect rented gear for zips and warmth before you set off.
